name: Pitch
tagline: Build structured presentations with reusable blocks, comments, and polished export

pricing.notes: Advertised annual-equivalent seat price; monthly billing is higher.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 1–5 members; 100 one-time AI credits; 2 external guests; 10 GB total storage; 1 teamspace.

tiers.name: Plus
tiers.limits: Maximum 1 member; 500 AI credits/month; 5 external guests; 10 GB storage.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: 1–25 members; 500 AI credits per seat/month pooled across the workspace; 25 advanced links; 3 teamspaces; 2 rooms; 25 guests; 10 GB/member.

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: 1–200 members; 750 AI credits per seat/month pooled across the workspace; unlimited advanced links, teamspaces, rooms and guests; 10 GB/member.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: For 30+ seats with SSO/SCIM, invoicing and custom support; price is not public.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1–5 members, 100 one-time AI credits, 2 guests, 10 GB total storage and 1 teamspace.
pricing.hiddenCosts: Member caps count paid and free roles. AI credits renew with the subscription and are pooled across the workspace, so heavy users can consume the team's allowance.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Pitch, build structured presentations with reusable blocks, comments, and polished export. The hard boundary is real-time collaboration, templates, analytics, and team content management, plus editor polish, assets, collaboration, and distribution.
coreLoopDIY: Build structured presentations from reusable blocks on a canvas, edit text and media, support comments, and export a finished deck as SVG or PDF.
whatYouLose: real-time collaboration, templates, analytics, and team content management
moatNotes: editor polish, assets, collaboration, and distribution
ongoingBurden: canvas correctness, fonts, exports, templates, asset rights, multiplayer state, and accessibility
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Pitch because people pay for a vast ready-made design system and a collaboration surface that behaves predictably under deadline. The recurring cost buys canvas correctness, fonts, exports, templates, asset rights, multiplayer state, and accessibility, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Penpot
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source collaborative design platform with SVG-native editing.

alternatives.name: Canva Free
alternatives.desc: Polished presentation templates and collaborative editing with good PDF export; more design playground, less structured deck system.

facts.install: Hosted signup in a browser, or install Canva's desktop/mobile app.
facts.engines: Canva AI and Magic Studio provide generative tools; Canva does not publish a complete provider/model map for the free editor.
facts.dataFormat: Designs, uploads, folders and brand assets live in Canva's cloud; users export common image, PDF, presentation and video formats.
facts.gapVsPaid: Canva is more of a free-form design playground and lacks Pitch's disciplined reusable blocks and deck-specific workflow.

alternatives.name: Google Slides
alternatives.desc: The boring default remains excellent: live collaboration, comments, templates, and PPTX/PDF export with no meaningful personal-use ceiling.

facts.install: Sign in with a Google account in a browser or install the mobile app; browser offline mode is optional.
facts.dataFormat: Presentations live in Google Drive and export to PPTX, PDF, ODP and other formats; offline copies can be cached locally.
facts.gapVsPaid: Google Slides collaborates well but produces less polished layouts and has a weaker reusable-block system than Pitch.

alternatives.name: LibreOffice Impress
alternatives.desc: A proper offline presentation app with PPTX/PDF support and no account; collaboration means sending files like it is 2012.

facts.install: Install the official MSI, DMG or Linux package.
facts.dataFormat: Presentations are local ODP files (zipped XML); Impress reads and writes PPTX and exports PDF.
facts.gapVsPaid: Impress has no native live web collaboration, comments workflow or shared workspace comparable to Pitch.

alternatives.name: Pitch Free
alternatives.desc: The same structured presentation editor for up to five people, with unlimited decks and templates; free PDFs carry Pitch branding and PPTX export is absent.

facts.install: Hosted signup in a browser, or install Pitch's desktop/mobile app.
facts.engines: Pitch AI uses external model providers; current public documentation does not identify exact models.
facts.dataFormat: Presentation data is stored in Pitch's AWS-hosted cloud, including database and object storage; PDF export is available.
facts.gapVsPaid: Pitch Free brands exported PDFs and does not provide PPTX export, two serious handoff limitations.

alternatives.name: PowerPoint for the web
alternatives.desc: Free browser PowerPoint with comments, coauthoring, and familiar file export; less elegant than Pitch, more likely to open everywhere.

facts.install: Sign in with a free Microsoft account and open PowerPoint in a browser.
facts.dataFormat: .pptx files live in OneDrive's free storage and can be downloaded or exported in supported formats.
facts.gapVsPaid: PowerPoint for the web is less elegant for structured reusable blocks and modern design automation than Pitch.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Penpot
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A design canvas can make slides one rectangle at a time, but it lacks presentation structure, playback, notes, and sane deck export.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Plus plan and a personal design canvas DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Pitch in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, IndexedDB, and SVG; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build structured presentations from reusable blocks on a canvas, edit text and media, support comments, and export a finished deck as SVG or PDF.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a fixed-size SVG canvas with zoom, pan, selection, alignment, and snapping.
Support text, rectangles, circles, images, groups, layers, and reusable components.
Add a small set of high-quality starter layouts relevant to the product category.
Implement undo, redo, autosave, and import or export of a portable project JSON file.
Export SVG and print-ready PDF without rasterizing text unnecessarily.
Keep all assets local and display missing-font warnings before export.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out real-time multiplayer editing.
Deliberately leave out a commercial stock-asset library.
Deliberately leave out enterprise brand controls and approval workflows.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
